cards.q: Why can two processes not share data by writing to the same address?
cards.a:
Each has its own private address space; the same address refers to different memory in each

Every process has its own virtual address space, so `0x2C409610` in one process and in another are unrelated memory (or nothing). That isolation is why IPC needs kernel-provided channels.

cards.q: Why is holding a process handle better than remembering its PID?
cards.a:
A PID can be reused once the process ends; a held handle cannot be

PIDs are recycled after a process is gone. While you hold a handle, the process object stays valid (you can still read its exit code) and its PID cannot be given to another process.

cards.q: Which of these is a list of ways processes on one machine can exchange data or signals?
cards.a:
Pipes, file mappings, sockets and named events

Anything that crosses processes must be provided by the OS: pipes, file mappings, sockets, named kernel objects, window messages and files. Global, `static` and thread-local variables live inside one address space.

cards.q: What happens to a pipe when the process at its other end crashes?
cards.a:
Windows closes its handles, so the pipe breaks and I/O on it fails

When a process ends, Windows closes every handle it held. The pipe's other end is then gone, so reads and writes on the surviving end fail; good IPC code plans for that.

cards.q: How does an environment block end?
cards.a:
Each `NAME=value` string ends with a zero, and the whole block ends with one more zero

Each string is zero-terminated and an extra zero marks the end of the block, so the block finishes with two zeros in a row.

cards.q: In what order must variables appear in an environment block?
cards.a:
Sorted by name, ignoring case

Windows expects the block sorted by name, case-insensitively. Names themselves are case-insensitive, so `Path` and `PATH` are the same variable and must not both appear.

cards.q: What goes wrong when `inheritHandles` is `TRUE` without a handle list in a multi-threaded program?
cards.a:
Every inheritable handle leaks in, even ones other threads just made

With inheritance on, every inheritable handle is copied into the child. A handle another thread creates at that moment leaks in too, so a pipe may never see end-of-file. `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST` limits it to the handles you name.

cards.q: Why start a child with `CREATE_SUSPENDED`?
cards.a:
To do something before it runs any code, such as adding it to a job object

The main thread is created paused; you can assign the process to a job (or anything else) and then call `ResumeThread`. Lower priority and no window are other flags (`BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS`, `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`).

cards.q: Why should a wait for a child process always have a timeout?
cards.a:
A hung child would otherwise freeze the parent indefinitely

A child stuck on a dialog, on input it never gets, or in a deadlock never ends, so an `INFINITE` wait would block the parent for ever. A timeout lets the parent decide to keep waiting or end it.

cards.q: A helper's exit code is `0xC0000005`. What happened?
cards.a:
It crashed with an access violation, an NTSTATUS error

`0xC...` codes are NTSTATUS errors: the process did not choose to exit. `0xC0000005` is an access violation; Ctrl+C is `0xC000013A`, and "still running" is `STILL_ACTIVE` (259).

cards.q: Why is `TerminateProcess` a last resort?
cards.a:
It ends the process at once, with no clean-up of any kind

`TerminateProcess` stops the process at once, so nothing gets a chance to clean up. Ask it to stop through your own channel first, wait a little, and terminate only if it does not.

cards.q: What does `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` give you?
cards.a:
Every process in the job is ended when the last job handle closes, even if the parent crashes

When the last handle to the job closes (including because the owning process crashed and Windows closed its handles), every process in the job is ended, so helpers do not outlive their parent.

cards.q: Why must the parent close its copy of the child's stdout write handle after starting it?
cards.a:
Otherwise a write handle stays open and the read never sees EOF

A pipe's reader sees end-of-file only when all write handles are closed. If the parent still holds `outWrite`, reading `outRead` waits for ever after the child exits.

cards.q: What is the stdout and stderr deadlock?
cards.a:
The parent waits on stdout while the child blocks on a full stderr

Each pipe has a fixed buffer. If the parent reads only stdout until end-of-file, a child that fills stderr blocks and never closes stdout. Read every output pipe continuously, for example one thread per pipe.

cards.q: Why can a single read return half a line?
cards.a:
Pipes carry bytes in arbitrary chunks; line boundaries are not preserved

A pipe is a byte stream: one read can return half a line or several. Keep a buffer per stream and take out complete lines as they arrive.

cards.q: How does the Language Server Protocol mark where a message ends?
cards.a:
A `Content-Length` header gives the size of the body after it

LSP sends headers, a blank line, then a body of the length the `Content-Length` header gave. The reader parses headers up to the blank line, then reads exactly that many bytes.

cards.q: Which method has no per-byte cost once set up, and what does it lack?
cards.a:
Shared memory; it lacks framing and synchronisation

Once a file mapping is mapped into both processes, nothing is copied per byte. But you build every structure and all synchronisation yourself, usually with events or a seqlock beside it.

cards.q: Which methods tell you automatically when the other side has died?
cards.a:
Pipes and sockets

Pipes and sockets close when the other process ends, so the next read or write fails. Shared memory just keeps the last data, so it needs its own liveness checks.

cards.q: Two unrelated programs need to talk. What do they need that a parent and child do not?
cards.a:
A name both know: a pipe name, a mapping name or a port number

A parent and its child can share anonymous pipes or inherited handles. Unrelated processes have no such handle to share, so they find each other through a name such as a named pipe, a named mapping or a port.

cards.q: Why might you choose sockets even when both processes are on one machine?
cards.a:
The same code then works across a network, in any language

Sockets cost a little more than pipes or shared memory locally, but the same code works remotely and every language has them. They are byte streams, so they still need framing.

cards.q: Two writes of 4 bytes each go into a pipe. What might a single read of 16 bytes return?
cards.a:
Anything from a few bytes up to all 8

An anonymous pipe is a byte stream: the read returns whatever is there, up to the buffer size, with no record of how it was written. It does not wait to fill the buffer.

cards.q: How does a reader of an anonymous pipe recognise end-of-file?
cards.a:
`ReadFile` fails with `ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE`

For a pipe, end-of-file is `ReadFile` failing with `ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE` (109) after every write handle is closed. `ERROR_NO_DATA` is what a writer sees when the read end has been closed.

cards.q: Why can't an unrelated program connect to an anonymous pipe?
cards.a:
It has no name; you can only be handed a handle to it

With no name there is nothing to open. Another process can use an end only if it is handed a handle, by inheritance at start-up or by `DuplicateHandle`.

cards.q: How do you check whether data is waiting without blocking?
cards.a:
`PeekNamedPipe` reports the number of bytes available

`PeekNamedPipe` works on anonymous pipes too and fills in the number of bytes waiting; a `ReadFile` of up to that many bytes then returns at once.

cards.q: What does one call to `CreateNamedPipeW` create?
cards.a:
One instance: a slot for one client at a time

Each call creates one instance, which serves one client at a time. To serve several clients at once, the server creates more instances of the same name.

cards.q: A client gets `ERROR_PIPE_BUSY`. What does it mean and what should it do?
cards.a:
Every instance is in use; wait with `WaitNamedPipeW` and retry

`ERROR_PIPE_BUSY` means every instance is taken. Wait with `WaitNamedPipeW` and loop, since another client can win the race. No server at all gives `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`.

cards.q: In message mode, what does `ERROR_MORE_DATA` on a read mean?
cards.a:
The message did not fit; the rest of it comes with the next read

In message mode each read returns at most one message. If it does not fit, you get what fits and `ERROR_MORE_DATA`; read again to get the rest of that same message.

cards.q: Are pipe names case-sensitive?
cards.a:
No, names differing only in case refer to the same pipe

Pipe names are not case-sensitive, and they are global to the machine, which is why names should be specific to the product, purpose and user.

cards.q: Why is a newline delimiter a poor choice for binary messages?
cards.a:
The newline byte can occur inside binary data and split a message

Binary data can contain any byte, including `\n`, so a delimiter would end the message early. A length prefix says how many bytes follow, whatever they are.

cards.q: A frame header says the payload is 3 000 000 000 bytes. What should the reader do?
cards.a:
Treat it as a protocol error, refuse to allocate, and close the connection

The length comes from another process and must not be trusted. Enforce a maximum suited to the protocol; anything above it is a protocol error that ends the connection.

cards.q: Why close the connection after a framing error rather than skip the bad message?
cards.a:
The reader no longer knows where the next frame starts

The only way to find the next frame is the length of this one. Once that is wrong, every later header would be read from the wrong place, so there is nothing safe to continue with.

cards.q: What must a message-mode reader do when a read fails with `ERROR_MORE_DATA`?
cards.a:
Read again and join the pieces of the same message

`ERROR_MORE_DATA` is not a failure of the message: the rest of it is still waiting. Read again and append until a read succeeds, still enforcing a maximum size.

cards.q: How does a pipe server handle three clients at the same time?
cards.a:
It creates three instances of the same pipe name, one per client

Each instance carries one connection. The accept loop creates a fresh instance, waits for a client on it, hands it to a thread, and creates the next one.

cards.q: Why might a client get `ERROR_PIPE_BUSY` even though the server serves unlimited clients?
cards.a:
Briefly, between accepting one client and the next instance, none is free

For a moment after `ConnectNamedPipe` returns, no instance is listening. A client arriving then waits with `WaitNamedPipeW` and gets in; some servers keep two instances listening to narrow the gap.

cards.q: When is a thread per client a poor choice?
cards.a:
With hundreds or thousands of clients

A thread per client is simple and right for tens of clients. For hundreds or thousands, their stacks and scheduling cost too much, and overlapped I/O with a completion port serves them all with a few threads.

cards.q: Why is the client's PID not proof of its identity?
cards.a:
PIDs are reused and any process may connect to the pipe

The PID is useful for logging and watching the client, but any program may connect and PIDs get reused. Security descriptors on the pipe are the real gate.

cards.q: What must stay alive until an overlapped operation completes?
cards.a:
The `OVERLAPPED` structure and the buffer passed to the call

The kernel writes into your buffer and `OVERLAPPED` when the operation finishes. If they were on the stack of a function that has returned, it corrupts memory.

cards.q: What does `ERROR_IO_PENDING` from `ReadFile` on an overlapped handle mean?
cards.a:
The read has started and will finish later

With overlapped I/O, `ReadFile` returns `FALSE` with `ERROR_IO_PENDING` to say the operation is in progress. The result comes later through `GetOverlappedResult`, the event or a completion port.

cards.q: What does the key passed to `CreateIoCompletionPort` give a worker thread?
cards.a:
Your own value, usually a pointer to the connection's state

You choose the key when you associate a handle with the port; `GetQueuedCompletionStatus` returns it with each completion, so the worker knows which connection the completion belongs to.

cards.q: Why do servers using completion ports structure connections as state machines?
cards.a:
Completions arrive one at a time, so each connection tracks its state

No thread runs one connection from top to bottom any more. A connection records its state (reading the header, the body, writing) and, on each completion, advances and starts the next operation.

cards.q: Why is shared memory faster than a pipe for large amounts of data?
cards.a:
Nothing is copied: both processes see the same physical pages

A pipe copies bytes from the sender into the kernel and again into the receiver. A file mapping puts the same physical pages in both address spaces, so a byte written by one is simply there for the other.

cards.q: Why is a pointer stored in shared memory useless to the other process?
cards.a:
The view is mapped at different addresses in each process

Each process's view appears at an address chosen independently, so the same bytes live at different addresses. Store offsets from the start of the block instead.

cards.q: What is the difference between `Local\name` and `Global\name`?
cards.a:
`Local` is per session; `Global` spans sessions and needs a privilege

Kernel object names live in a namespace per login session. `Global\` objects are shared across sessions (for example with a service in session 0), and creating them needs `SeCreateGlobalPrivilege`.

cards.q: When does a page-file backed mapping's content disappear?
cards.a:
When every handle and view in every process is gone

The mapping lives while any process holds a handle or a view. If the creator exits but another process still has it open, the data stays; once all are gone, the next creator gets fresh zeroed memory.

cards.q: Why store offsets instead of pointers in shared memory?
cards.a:
Views sit at different addresses; an offset means the same in each

A pointer is only valid at the address where this process's view sits. Each process turns an offset into a pointer locally with `base + offset`.

cards.q: Why is `std::string` unsuitable as a member of a shared struct?
cards.a:
It points into its own process's heap, which others cannot reach

A `std::string` (like `std::vector`) holds a pointer to memory in its own process's heap. Use fixed-size arrays such as `char name[64]`, or offsets to data inside the block.

cards.q: What are a shared header's magic number, version and size for?
cards.a:
To recognise the block, check its layout and bound its offsets

The magic number catches an unrelated or stale block, the version tells a reader whether it understands the layout, and the size lets it reject offsets that point past the end.

cards.q: Why must `std::atomic` be lock-free to work in shared memory?
cards.a:
A lock-based one uses a lock private to each process's runtime

A non-lock-free atomic falls back on a lock kept inside the process's runtime, so two processes would use two different locks. Check `is_always_lock_free`, and use named kernel objects instead of `std::mutex`.

cards.q: Why does an SPSC ring buffer need no lock?
cards.a:
Each counter has one writer: the producer or the consumer

No variable is ever written by both sides, so there is nothing to lock; acquire and release ordering on the counters is enough. With several producers or consumers this no longer holds.

cards.q: With ever-increasing counters, how do you test for full?
cards.a:
`head - tail == capacity`

The number of items is `head - tail`, so the ring is full when it equals the capacity. `head == tail` means empty, and comparing the slot indexes cannot tell full from empty.

cards.q: Why must the producer store the new `head` with release ordering after writing the slot?
cards.a:
So a consumer that sees the new `head` also sees the slot's data

Release on the store and acquire on the load pair up: every write before the release (the slot) is visible to a thread that sees the stored value. Without it the consumer could read a stale slot.

cards.q: Why are ring capacities usually powers of two?
cards.a:
The slot index becomes a cheap mask, `counter & (capacity - 1)`

With a power of two, `n % capacity` is a cheap mask, and since the counter's range is a multiple of the capacity, slots stay in order when the counter wraps past its maximum.

cards.q: Why is mapping a 2 GB file and reading a few bytes from its end fast?
cards.a:
Pages are read only when touched, so only the pages actually read are loaded

Mapping just sets up the address range; each page is read from disk the first time it is accessed. Reading a few bytes touches one or two pages.

cards.q: You want a view starting at file offset 200 000. Where must the view actually start?
cards.a:
At 196 608, the 64 KB boundary below; the data is 3 392 bytes in

A view's offset must be a multiple of the 64 KB allocation granularity, so round down to 196 608 and skip `200 000 - 196 608 = 3 392` bytes into the view. Rounding up would miss the data.

cards.q: How do you make sure written data has reached the disk?
cards.a:
`FlushViewOfFile`, then `FlushFileBuffers` on the file

The OS writes changed pages back in its own time. `FlushViewOfFile` starts writing them; `FlushFileBuffers` waits until they are really on the disk.

cards.q: How does a disk error show up when reading through a mapped file?
cards.a:
As an `EXCEPTION_IN_PAGE_ERROR` structured exception at the memory access

The error happens when a page is touched, inside an ordinary memory access, so it arrives as a structured exception. Code mapping files it does not control wraps access in `__try` / `__except`.

cards.q: What is a torn read?
cards.a:
A mix of old and new state that never existed as a whole

If a reader copies while the writer is halfway through, it may get the new x with the old y. A seqlock detects that and retries.

cards.q: What does an odd sequence counter tell a seqlock reader?
cards.a:
A write is in progress, so it must try again

The writer makes the counter odd before writing and even again after. An odd value means the data is being changed right now.

cards.q: Why does the reader read the counter a second time after copying?
cards.a:
If it changed, a write overlapped the copy, which may be torn

The reader never writes the counter. Comparing it before and after the copy shows whether a write overlapped the copy; if so, the reader retries.

cards.q: Why is a seqlock better than a mutex for a game publishing state to a tool?
cards.a:
The writer never waits, so a slow tool cannot slow the game

With a lock, a reader holding it would make the game wait. A seqlock's writer never blocks; readers retry only when they overlapped a write. It still allows only one writer.

cards.q: Two programs both call `CreateEventW` with the same name. What happens to the second call?
cards.a:
It opens the existing event and succeeds, with `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS`

`Create...` opens an existing object of that name and still succeeds, so either side may start first. Read `GetLastError()` straight away to learn whether you created it.

cards.q: When should a program use `OpenEventW` instead of `CreateEventW`?
cards.a:
When it must fail if nobody created the object yet

`Open...` fails with `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` if nobody created the object, which is exactly what a client wants: it must not create the server's objects and then wait on them for ever.

cards.q: When is a mutex signalled?
cards.a:
When no thread owns it

A mutex is signalled while unowned; a successful wait makes the waiter the owner and the mutex non-signalled. An owner dying also releases it, but as abandoned.

cards.q: When does a named kernel object disappear?
cards.a:
When the last handle to it, in any process, is closed

A kernel object lives as long as any process holds a handle. If the creator exits while another process has it open, it stays and keeps its state.

cards.q: When should an event be manual-reset rather than auto-reset?
cards.a:
When it marks a state, like "stopping", for all waiters

A manual-reset event wakes every waiter and stays set until `ResetEvent`, so it suits a state like "stopping". Auto-reset lets one waiter through per set, which suits "there is work".

cards.q: `SetEvent` is called three times on an auto-reset event before the consumer wakes. How many times does the consumer's wait succeed?
cards.a:
Once: an event is a flag, not a counter

Setting an event that is already set does nothing. Once woken, the consumer must process everything waiting. To count signals, use a semaphore.

cards.q: How can a consumer of shared memory find out that the producer process has died?
cards.a:
Also wait on the producer's process handle, signalled when it ends

Shared memory never tells you its peer has gone, and an event a dead process will never set just stays unset. A process handle is signalled when the process ends. Only mutexes are abandoned.

cards.q: With `bWaitAll` `FALSE`, which index is returned if two handles are signalled at once?
cards.a:
The lowest one, so the most important handle should come first

`WaitForMultipleObjects` reports the lowest signalled index. Put "stop" first so it wins when it arrives together with data.

cards.q: What does `WAIT_ABANDONED` mean on a mutex wait?
cards.a:
You own it, but its last owner died holding it; check the data

Windows releases a mutex whose owner died and marks it abandoned. The next waiter owns it but must validate or repair the data, then still call `ReleaseMutex`.

cards.q: Why is a Win32 mutex called recursive?
cards.a:
Its owner can wait on it again, releasing once per wait

The owner can re-acquire without deadlocking itself, but it must release once per successful wait. Only the owning thread may release; others get `ERROR_NOT_OWNER`.

cards.q: Why is there no abandonment for semaphores?
cards.a:
A semaphore has no owner, so nobody is known to hold a slot

Taking a slot records nobody as its holder. If a process dies holding one, the count is simply lost, which is why long-running systems track slots themselves.

cards.q: A semaphore created with initial count 4 and maximum 4 has five waiters. How many get through at once?
cards.a:
Four; the fifth waits until one releases

Each successful wait takes one from the count, blocking at 0. Four waits succeed, and the fifth proceeds after a `ReleaseSemaphore`.

cards.q: Why can a normal message not carry a pointer to data for another process?
cards.a:
The pointer is only valid in the sender's address space

Each process has its own address space, so a pointer from the sender means nothing to the receiver. `WM_COPYDATA` is the exception because Windows copies the data across.

cards.q: How long is the data of a `WM_COPYDATA` message valid in the receiver?
cards.a:
Only while the receiver is handling the message

Windows copies the block in for the duration of the call only. That is also why `WM_COPYDATA` must be sent, not posted.

cards.q: Why use `SendMessageTimeoutW` rather than `SendMessageW` to another program?
cards.a:
A hung receiver would otherwise hang the sender indefinitely

`SendMessageW` waits until the receiver has processed the message. With a timeout (and `SMTO_ABORTIFHUNG`), a hung receiver costs at most the timeout.

cards.q: Why might `WM_COPYDATA` from a normal program never reach a program running as administrator?
cards.a:
UIPI drops it unless the elevated program allows that message

User Interface Privilege Isolation silently drops most messages to higher-integrity windows. The elevated program can allow one with `ChangeWindowMessageFilterEx`, and must then distrust its senders.

cards.q: What shape does a deadlock have in a wait-for graph?
cards.a:
A cycle: each waits for the next, the last for the first

Arrows go from each waiter to the holder of what it wants. A deadlock is a cycle; many waiters on one healthy holder is only contention.

cards.q: How does a global lock order prevent lock-order deadlocks?
cards.a:
Everyone takes locks in increasing rank, so no cycle can form

If locks are always taken lowest rank first, every wait-for arrow points "up" the ranking, so arrows can never loop back into a cycle.

cards.q: Why should a lock never be held during a pipe write or `SendMessage`?
cards.a:
A slow or hung peer then blocks everyone waiting for the lock

The write or send can block on the peer, so the lock stays held for as long as the peer takes. Copy what you need, release the lock, then do the IPC.

cards.q: An event the other process should set never arrives. Why should the wait have a timeout?
cards.a:
The other process may have died; a timeout lets you check

An event a dead process will never set just stays unset. After a timeout, wait on the peer's process handle with a 0 timeout to see if it is alive, then decide.

cards.q: Why bind a local IPC server to `127.0.0.1` rather than `0.0.0.0`?
cards.a:
`0.0.0.0` is reachable from the network; `127.0.0.1` only locally

Bound to all interfaces, a private endpoint is reachable from the network. Loopback limits it to this machine, but still to every local process, so the protocol must check who is talking.

cards.q: Why bind to port 0?
cards.a:
The system picks a free port, so nothing collides

Port 0 asks the system for any free port; `getsockname` then tells you which one you got. A fixed number can collide with another program or a second copy of yours.

cards.q: How does a client find a server that bound to port 0?
cards.a:
The server writes the port, its PID and a token to a known file

The port changes every run, so the server publishes it, for example in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Xenon\agent.port`, along with a token the client must present. `getsockname` only works on the server's own socket.

cards.q: What controls who may connect to an `AF_UNIX` socket?
cards.a:
The permissions of its path in the file system

An `AF_UNIX` endpoint is a file system path, so the folder's and file's permissions decide who can reach it. Loopback TCP is the one with no access control.

cards.q: What is the magic number in a handshake for?
cards.a:
To spot at once a peer that does not speak this protocol

A port scanner, a browser or an old program can connect to your endpoint. A fixed magic number at the start catches that at once; the version field, not the magic, says which dialect.

cards.q: A client speaks 2.3 and the server 2.1. Which version do they use?
cards.a:
2.1: the same major version and the lower minor version

Minor versions add features compatibly, so both sides agree on the lower minor and avoid newer features. Only a different major version means they cannot talk at all.

cards.q: Why do all messages share one envelope?
cards.a:
So generic code can frame, route and log any message

The envelope's length, type, flags and id are the same for every message, so generic code can frame, dispatch, match replies and log, leaving the payload to type-specific code.

cards.q: What should a receiver do with a request type it does not know?
cards.a:
Reply "not supported" and carry on with the connection

A newer sender may use types an older receiver lacks. A request still deserves a reply, so the client is not left waiting; unknown events can simply be ignored.

cards.q: Why not send a struct's raw bytes?
cards.a:
Padding, type sizes and heap pointers can differ between the sides

Raw memory depends on the compiler, the platform and the version: padding, `long`'s size, a `std::string`'s heap pointer, added fields. Serialise each value in a defined format instead.

cards.q: Encode 300 as a varint.
cards.a:
`AC 02`

300 is `0b10_0101100`. The low 7 bits `0101100` (0x2C) with the "more" bit become `0xAC`; the remaining bits `10` are `0x02`. `2C 01` is 300 as a plain little-endian 16-bit number.

cards.q: Why zigzag-encode signed numbers before writing them as varints?
cards.a:
Negatives would take ten bytes; zigzag keeps small ones short

In two's complement a small negative number has all its high bits set, so as a varint it takes ten bytes. Zigzag maps 0, -1, 1, -2, ... to 0, 1, 2, 3, ..., keeping small values short.

cards.q: How does tag-length-value let old readers handle new fields?
cards.a:
They skip any tag they do not know by its length and continue with the next field

Every field carries its own length, so an unknown tag can be skipped exactly. That is what lets a newer sender add fields without breaking older receivers.

cards.q: How does a client match a response to its request?
cards.a:
By the id it sent, echoed back

Each request carries an id unique among the client's outstanding requests; the response returns it, so the client finds the pending entry whatever order responses come in.

cards.q: What should a client do with a response whose id matches no pending request?
cards.a:
Log it and drop it: it is probably a late answer

After a timeout the client removes the request from its table, so a late answer matches nothing. It is expected occasionally, not a reason to drop the connection.

cards.q: Does one connection guarantee responses arrive in the order requests were sent?
cards.a:
No: a concurrent server may answer requests in any order

The stream keeps the order the server sends in, but the server may answer a quick request before a slow one. Clients should rely on ids, never on response order.

cards.q: Which of these is safe to retry blindly: `setVolume(70)` or `appendLog("x")`?
cards.a:
`setVolume(70)`, because it is idempotent

Doing `setVolume(70)` twice leaves the same result as once. A non-idempotent request needs a request key the server recognises, or the uncertainty reported to the user.

cards.q: What does `FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE` protect against?
cards.a:
Pipe squatting: an impostor creating the pipe's name first

Without the flag, a server whose name was taken first would just create another instance of the impostor's pipe. With it, creation fails and the server knows something is wrong. Remote clients are blocked by `PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS`.

cards.q: Why do localhost TCP servers need a token?
cards.a:
Any local process, and web pages, can reach a localhost port

Localhost ports have no access control. A random token stored in a file only the user can read is something other users, malware without access and web pages cannot present.

cards.q: How does checking the `Host` header defend against DNS rebinding?
cards.a:
A rebinding request carries the attacker's domain in `Host`

The browser connects to `127.0.0.1` but still sends the attacker's domain in `Host`. A server that accepts only `localhost:PORT` or `127.0.0.1:PORT` turns it away.

cards.q: Why should a client open an untrusted pipe with `SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION`?
cards.a:
So the server can identify the client but not impersonate it

A malicious server could call `ImpersonateNamedPipeClient` and act as the client. The identification level lets it see who the client is, but not act with the client's rights.

cards.q: How does a launched copy know another instance is already running?
cards.a:
`CreateMutexW` on the shared name succeeds with `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS`

Creating an existing named object opens it and succeeds, with `GetLastError()` set to `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS`. The mutex is never locked; only its existence matters.

cards.q: Why must the secondary send its current directory with the arguments?
cards.a:
Its relative paths mean nothing in the primary's folder

`notes.md` or `..\docs\a.md` only mean something relative to where the secondary was started. Send the directory so the primary can resolve them, or resolve them before sending.

cards.q: Why call `AllowSetForegroundWindow` in the secondary?
cards.a:
It hands the primary the right to take the foreground

Background processes may not steal the foreground. The secondary, just launched by the user, may, and passes that right on; otherwise the primary's window only flashes in the taskbar.

cards.q: Why should the secondary retry forwarding for a short time?
cards.a:
The primary may not have created its pipe or window yet

The kernel guarantees only one process creates the mutex, but the primary still needs time to create its pipe or window. A short retry covers that gap.

cards.q: Which pair are both reasons to run work in a separate process instead of a thread?
cards.a:
Crash isolation and running with fewer rights

Processes give crash isolation, memory isolation, fewer rights and parallel work without shared state. They cost more to start and to talk to than threads.

cards.q: Why use exponential backoff for restarts?
cards.a:
So a worker that crashes at start-up does not restart in a tight loop

Restarting at once for ever turns a crash at start-up into hundreds of restarts a second. Delays of 1, 2, 4, 8 s up to a cap retry quickly for transient faults and stop hammering for persistent ones.

cards.q: When should a supervisor stop restarting a worker?
cards.a:
After too many failures in a short time, such as 5 in 10 minutes

A burst of failures means something is persistently wrong. Mark the feature unavailable and tell someone. A clean exit with code 0 is not a failure and is not restarted.

cards.q: Why must the heartbeat come from the worker's main work loop?
cards.a:
A timer thread could tick on while the real work is hung

The heartbeat should prove the work is progressing. A timer thread keeps ticking even when the work loop is stuck, so the supervisor would never notice the hang.

cards.q: What does running a plugin out of process protect the host from?
cards.a:
Its crashes, hangs and memory corruption

A separate process contains crashes and corruption, and the host can stop it. It does not stop the plugin from using the user's rights; that needs a restricted token or sandbox.

cards.q: Why read a manifest before starting a plugin?
cards.a:
To check it is compatible without running its code

The manifest tells the host whether the API version is compatible, which events to send and which commands it offers, so the host can start plugins only when first needed.

cards.q: A plugin times out on three commands in a minute. What should the host do?
cards.a:
Disable it and tell the user which plugin was at fault

Count failures per plugin and disable one that keeps failing, naming it so the user knows what to update or remove. The host must stay responsive whatever plugins do.

cards.q: Why is a separate process alone not a security boundary against a malicious plugin?
cards.a:
It still has the user's rights and can read the user's files

Isolation protects against faults, not intent. A plugin running as the user can do whatever the user can; a low-integrity token or AppContainer forces everything through the host's checked API.

cards.q: Why separate framing and protocol logic from the transport?
cards.a:
So they can be tested quickly with byte vectors, without real pipes

Layers let the deframer and the protocol logic be unit-tested in milliseconds with byte vectors; a thin integration test then checks that the real transport is wired up.

cards.q: Which of these is a set of faults a fault-injecting transport should simulate?
cards.a:
Split and joined messages, dropped connections and garbage input

The IPC faults worth simulating are split and joined messages, delays and reordering, dropped connections, a killed peer and garbage such as absurd lengths and unknown types.

cards.q: Why normalise a transcript before comparing it with the golden one?
cards.a:
Timestamps and generated ids change on every run

Fields that legitimately change each run would make every comparison fail. Normalised, the test catches real protocol changes, including accidental ones.

cards.q: Which tool shows the named pipes, events and mutexes a process has open?
cards.a:
Process Explorer's handle view

Process Explorer's lower pane lists every handle a process holds, by name, and "Find Handle or DLL" finds who holds an object. Wireshark shows traffic, not handles.

cards.q: Why does a browser move rendered frames through shared memory rather than pipes?
cards.a:
Frames are large, and shared memory avoids copying them

Frames are big, and a pipe copies every byte twice. Shared memory moves them with no copying, and the pipes carry the small messages saying a frame is ready.

cards.q: What makes the Language Server Protocol usable from any editor and any language?
cards.a:
It is a documented protocol, not a library for one language

Because it is a protocol over stdio with JSON messages, a server written in any language works with any editor that speaks it.

cards.q: Why can a service and a tray application not use a `Local\` event to talk?
cards.a:
They run in different sessions, and `Local\` names are per session

A service runs in session 0 and the tray app in the user's session; `Local\` names are separate in each. They use a named pipe with a suitable security descriptor (or `Global\` objects) instead.

cards.q: Which of the seven design questions covers heartbeats and abandoned mutexes?
cards.a:
What fails, and how do you notice?

Heartbeats, timeouts, process handles and abandoned mutexes are all ways of noticing failure. Abuse is about access control, tokens and validation.
